lessons.title: What quality means on the farm
lessons.html:
What quality means on the farm

Quality means that a product meets the standard the buyer expects. A buyer pays more for good quality and may reject a whole load if it does not meet the standard. Export markets, retailers and processors have strict specifications. Quality also includes food safety: the product must be free of harmful germs, chemical residues above the legal limits, and foreign objects.

Who sets quality standards?

  • The law: the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 sets grading standards for many products sold in or exported from South Africa. Inspectors check export fruit and other regulated products.
  • Buyers: retailers, exporters and processors give specifications (specs).
  • Certification schemes: many farms follow schemes such as GLOBALG.A.P. or SIZA, with rules on food safety, worker welfare and the environment.
  • The farm: its own quality procedures and checklists.

What is checked?

ProductExamples of quality checks
FruitSize, colour, ripeness, sugar, blemishes, bruises, pest damage, rot
VegetablesSize, freshness, firmness, cleanliness, no yellow leaves
GrainMoisture, foreign matter, broken kernels, insect damage, mould
EggsClean, uncracked shells, correct size grade
MilkTemperature, no antibiotic residues, cleanliness
WoolClean, free of plastic and twine, correctly classed

Quality starts in the field

Quality cannot be added in the pack house; it can only be kept. Good pruning, irrigation, pest control, careful picking and gentle handling all create quality. Every worker is responsible for quality, not only the quality controller.

Poor quality has a real cost. A rejected load means lost income for the farm, wasted inputs and labour, and it can damage the farm's name with the buyer.

lessons.title: How to do a quality check and act on the results
lessons.html:
How to do a quality check and act on the results

Steps in a quality check

  1. Know the standard. Have the specification or checklist with you: what is acceptable and what is not. Many pack houses have photo charts of defects.
  2. Take a sample. Check a set number of items, taken at random from different places in the load, crate or bin, not only from the top.
  3. Inspect. Look, measure, weigh or test each item. Use the tools provided: size rings, colour charts, scales, thermometers, refractometers, moisture meters.
  4. Record. Write down the date, time, batch or block number, sample size, and the number and type of defects.
  5. Decide. Compare results with the standard: accept, re-sort, downgrade or reject.
  6. Report. Tell your supervisor about problems at once, with the numbers.

Example

A citrus picking team brings in bins. The quality controller samples 50 fruit from one bin and finds 6 with picking damage (clipper cuts and stem pulled out). That is 6 / 50 x 100 = 12%. If the farm's limit is lower than this, the supervisor must speak to the team at once, check their clippers and show the correct method, before more fruit is damaged.

Traceability

Every batch must be labelled so it can be traced back to the block, the picking date, and sometimes the team. If a problem is found later, for example a chemical residue, the farm can find the cause and remove only the affected product.

Calibrating tools

Measuring tools must be accurate. Check scales with a known weight, thermometers in iced water, and refractometers with clean water, as the farm's procedure says. Record the check.

Good practice

  • Be honest and consistent. Do not pass a bad batch because of pressure to finish.
  • Keep samples and records as the procedure says.
  • Look for causes, not only defects: if many fruit are bruised, check how bins are filled and moved.
  • Keep your work area and tools clean.

Key points

  • Quality means meeting the buyer's and legal standard, including food safety.
  • Standards come from the law, buyers, certification schemes and the farm.
  • Quality is created in the field and kept by careful handling.
  • Sample at random, inspect against the spec, record, decide and report.
  • Label batches for traceability and keep measuring tools calibrated.
